answers.q1: Because concatenating the op name and the canonical arguments without lengths lets two different (op, args) pairs produce the same bytes, i.e. the same id; the originating project writes a 32-bit length before the op name and before the canonical JSON, as goja-cv does with SHA-256.
answers.q2: No. The chapter says the node id is not the cache key; the cache key must add whatever else determines the result's pixels — scale, region and precision (`id | scale | region | precision`).
answers.q3: Keys built from input keys cannot cut off early: a change below always changes every name above, even when the change below produced identical pixels. If that matters, add output hashes (a verifying trace) at chosen checkpoints.
answers.q4: The sender sends `closure(target)`, the list of node definitions `{ op, inputs, args }` that the target depends on, with inputs before their users; the receiver calls `adopt`, which re-interns each definition, and because the hash is a pure function of those bytes it arrives at the same ids.

unclear: The paragraph never says the id must depend on nothing but the hashed bytes — no per-graph counter, no salt, no build number — yet that is the actual reason two processes reach the same id; the reader has to infer it from note 1 and the Collaborations section.

'replace node references by their ids' (Solution) directly conflicts with note 3, which says a node-typed argument must also be appended to the inputs; from the Solution alone a reader cannot tell whether the reference belongs only in the args or in both places.

'Send graphs between processes as the list of node definitions in a target's closure' — 'target' is overloaded here: it means the node whose closure you take, while two sentences later 'target' means scale/region/precision. Use 'the requested node' for the first sense.

The ordering contract of `closure` (inputs before users) and of `adopt` (re-intern in that order) appears only in the sketch, not in the Solution or Collaborations prose, so the transfer rule reads as magic.

The Solution never says whether the Graph is per-compile or session-long, so a reader cannot tell whether reuse comes from the intern map or from the separate result cache (the sketch reuses one `g` across three compiles, which silently answers the question).

Forward references ('see Chapter 5' inside the sketch, Chapter 2/7/9/12 in Related chapters) interrupt the argument at exactly the two points where the reader most needs a sentence of local explanation.
Nothing says which hash function or id encoding is canonical (hex string, raw bytes, 52-bit number); note 7 offers three different widths without stating the default.

'Fine names against coarse caches' and note 5 say essentially the same thing in two vocabularies, leaving the reader unsure whether a node id plus a target is a pair, a struct, or a composite key string.

'the agent's sandbox, the GPU worker and the main thread' in the Motivation assumes a process topology the reader has not been shown; a new reader cannot tell whether that is three processes or three threads.
'Editor lab' and 'goja-cv' appear in Implementation notes and Known uses with no one-line gloss of what they are, so the reader cannot weigh the evidence.
errors: The sketch breaks its own rule 1: `concat(inputs)` appends input ids with no length prefix, so ids ('1','23') and ('12','3') hash identically. Either state that ids are fixed-width and therefore self-delimiting, or length-prefix each input id.

If a node-typed argument is replaced by its id *only* in the args (as the Solution says), the scheduler and `closure` do not see the edge — note 3 exists precisely to fix this, so the Solution as written is an implementable bug.

The collision figure is right (birthday bound n²/2^(k+1) ≈ 10¹⁰/2⁵³ ≈ 1.1×10⁻⁶ at 52 bits and 10⁵ keys) but it is presented bare, without the formula or whether that is per project, per session or per lookup — readers will assume per lookup and be confused about why anyone accepts it.

'Value numbering in compilers is the same idea' overstates it: GVN reasons about computed values and congruence within a scope and does not give transferable names; the honest claim is that it is the same family of idea, not the same technique.

'libvips caches operations keyed by the operation and its arguments' is doubtful as listed next to Git and Nix/Bazel: libvips's operation cache is a small, bounded, in-process LRU, so it is not a content-addressed identity that travels between processes the way the surrounding entries are. Either qualify it as 'in-process reuse only' or drop it.

The Solution's claim that immutability makes evaluation lock-free is stated in Consequences without noting that interning itself is a shared mutable map and needs a lock or a single writer; as written it invites an unsafe parallel implementation.
missing: Deterministic serialisation of floats: `-0 → 0` is mentioned, but not 1 vs 1.0, 1e21 vs 1e+21, 0.1+0.2 vs 0.3, NaN payloads, or quantisation of parameters to a fixed number of decimals. This is the single most common real cause of 'same computation, different id'.

Versioning: a change to a registry default or to a normalisation rule silently renames every node and invalidates every cache; there is no schema/hash-version tag in the id and no advice on what to do when it must change.
Cache lifecycle for the result cache: no size bound, no eviction policy, no statement that a graph entry can be evicted without changing ids (q5 is unanswerable from the chapter).

Collision handling beyond 'use a wide hash': the obvious mitigations (store the canonical byte string beside the node and compare on hit; visible-length id plus full hash) are never offered, even though a collision is called a silently wrong picture.
Cycles: interning bottom-up assumes a DAG; nothing says `intern`/`adopt` must refuse a cycle or how.
Concurrency of `intern` itself (two threads, or a worker and the main thread, interning at once) and whether `adopt` may merge into a graph that already contains some of the definitions.
Cost of the interning hash in absolute terms, so a reader can check the 'negligible for tens of nodes, measurable for per-tile keys' claim against their own graphs.
review.too_long: Two places. (a) The Solution is one four-clause paragraph carrying six distinct rules (intern through one path, canonicalise, hash, dedupe, immutability, transfer, cache key) and reads as a checklist rather than an argument. (b) Its concrete form is then restated: note 5 repeats the 'Fine names against coarse caches' force *and* the Result-cache row of the Structure table; note 9 repeats the Consequences bullet 'Names built from inputs cannot express unchanged output'; note 7 repeats the cheap/safe force. Roughly two of the ten notes are pure duplication, and the notes are the longest section in the chapter.
suggested_edits: Split the Solution into four short labelled sentences: (1) identity — one `intern` path, canonicalise, hash op + args + input ids, dedupe; (2) immutability; (3) transfer — `closure` sends definitions, `adopt` re-interns, ids agree because the hash sees nothing else; (4) cache key — node id *plus* the evaluation target.

Repair the sketch so it obeys note 1: `id ← hash(fp(opName) ++ fp(json(args)) ++ concat(fp(i) for i in inputs))`, and state once, above it, that `fp(x)` is a 32-bit length prefix or a fixed-width field (fixed-width ids make the concatenation self-delimiting).

Make the Solution agree with note 3 by appending to 'replace node references by their ids': '— and append that id to the node's inputs, so the hash covers the dependency and the scheduler sees the edge.'

Add to the Solution: 'The id depends on nothing else — no counter, no per-graph salt, no build number — which is why a second process lands on the same id; consequently any change to a default or a normalisation rule is an id/schema version bump.'

Add one lifecycle sentence: the Graph may be per-compile or session-long, but the result cache is a separate evictable map keyed by `(id, target)`; evicting entries never changes ids, and state the eviction policy (LRU over checkpoints, Chapter 7) explicitly.

Fold note 5 into the Structure table's Result-cache row and keep note 6 (cache granularity / checkpoints), which is the only place the 'interning makes caching possible, not automatic' point is actionable; cross-reference note 9 from Consequences instead of repeating it.

Give note 7 a policy sentence instead of three anecdotes: 'prefer 256-bit ids; if you must fit a number, 52 bits means ~1 in 10⁶ projects sees one collision, so accept it only where a wrong frame is cheap, and store the canonical bytes beside the node to make a detected collision recoverable.'

Add a short canonical-bytes subsection: JSON keys sorted, numbers formatted by one routine (or quantised to N decimals), -0 → 0, NaN refused, node refs forbidden in args (they go to inputs), and one worked byte string shown as a hex example so the length prefixes are visible.
Say in Collaborations that `closure` returns a topological order (inputs before users) and that `adopt` re-interns in that order and refuses cycles and unknown ops with a fix-it message.

Gloss the projects on first use — 'the originating project (a browser-based print-simulation editor)', 'Editor lab', 'goja-cv (a Go computer-vision pipeline)' — and replace 'the agent's sandbox, the GPU worker and the main thread' with the concrete process/time topology so the transfer argument lands.

Qualify or drop libvips in Known uses ('libvips reuses completed operations through a small in-process cache keyed by operation and arguments — the same idea without transferable ids'), and soften the value-numbering sentence to 'the same idea in compiler form'.

applications.context: Node-based compositing tool for VFX (Read, Grade, Keyer, Blur, Merge), artists tweaking interactively, final frames rendered on a farm of many machines.

participants.Operation registry: the comp node-type registry: one entry per node type (Read, Grade, Keyer, Blur, Merge) with its parameter specs, defaults and animation channels
participants.Canonicaliser: canonical serialisation of a node's parameters: sorted keys, defaults bound, floats quantised to a fixed decimal grid, colour values in one working space, file/sequence references reduced to a content stamp, node references replaced by ids and moved to the input list
participants.Graph: the comp's node DAG, kept alive for the editing session (and its id→node map persisted so farm blades can be handed closures)
participants.Node: an interned compositing op with inferred info: output resolution, proxy level, channels, pixel aspect
participants.Node definition: the serialised `{op, inputs, args}` list inside the render job packet shipped to each blade
participants.Result cache: per-blade and object-storage render cache keyed by `(id, frame, full-res|proxy level, tile region, bit depth, working colour space, sampling/precision)`

applications.sketch:
read = intern(g,'Read',[],{path:'plate.exr', stamp: {size, mtime, contentHash}, first:1001, last:1100, frame: f})
grade = intern(g,'Grade',[read],{gain:[1,1,1], lift:[0,0,0], gamma:2.2})
key   = intern(g,'Keyer',[grade],{screen:'green', tol:0.12})
bg    = intern(g,'Blur',[grade],{radius:12, passes:3})
out   = intern(g,'Merge',[bg,key],{op:'over'})

-- per frame on the artist's machine (proxy) and on the farm (full res)
key0 = (out.id, f, 'proxy', fullRegion, 8, 'sRGB', 'f32')
if cache.has(key0): show cache.get(key0) else: img = eval(out, 'proxy'); cache.put(key0, img)

-- farm: submit job
send job = { defs: closure(g, out.id), frames: 1001..1100, target: 'full' }
blade: g2 = new Graph; adopt(g2, job.defs);   assert g2[out.id].id == out.id
for f in job.frames: emit full_res(g2, out.id, f)
applications.key_note: Note 6, cache granularity: the originating project caches only whole final images, and the farm's whole cost model is re-running every stage from Read on the next tweak. Interning gives identical ids across blades and across DCC sessions — that is what makes a shared intermediate cache possible — but it does not create one; you must deliberately designate checkpoints (which node ids to persist per frame) or you get none of the reuse.
applications.failure_or_adaptation: Time is a hidden input here: an animated parameter or a frame-dependent node makes every frame share an id unless the frame is baked into the canonical args or supplied as an explicit time input node (note 8). External media is the classic stale-result trap — a plate re-exported under the same path — so the Read node must hash a content stamp, not the path. Plugin or DCC version changes alter canonicalisation and silently rename everything, so carry a schema/generator version in the hash. Roto and key tweaks are frequent masked edits where input-key names over-invalidate (33–52 % avoidable work in the chapter's measurement), so if incremental re-render matters, add Merkle tile keys or verifying traces at checkpoints. Non-deterministic GPU ops (uninitialised memory, atomics, DoF jitter) break the premise that equal id plus equal target means equal pixels; those ops must take their seeds as arguments. Farm-scale caches also need eviction that respects checkpoint semantics and per-shot pinning, and id equality is only useful if every blade runs the same hash and float formatting — a locale or library skew is a silent split-brain.

applications.context: WebGPU shader-graph material editor in the browser deciding which shader variants to compile, cache and reuse as users edit material graphs.

participants.Operation registry: the shader-node library (texture sample, maths, remap, blend, normal map) with parameter specs, defaults and the WGSL emission rule for each node
participants.Canonicaliser: canonical node parameters plus deterministic WGSL text emission (stable identifier names, stable declaration order) and uniform-buffer layout
participants.Graph: the material graph, interned live as the user drags sliders, kept for the session and serialised into the asset
participants.Node: an interned shader-graph node with inferred info: value type and dimensionality (f32/vec3f/vec4f), required bindings, emitted expression
participants.Node definition: the `{op, inputs, args}` list stored in the material asset, handed to a compile worker (worker thread or the main thread) for re-interning
participants.Result cache: compiled-variant cache keyed by `(interface id, WGSL feature set, backend/adapter, precision f16|f32, render-pass state: target formats, blend, depth, sample count)`, persisted in IndexedDB on top of the browser's own pipeline cache

applications.sketch:
albedoTex = intern(g,'TexSample',[],{slot:'albedo', uv:0, wrap:'repeat'})
rough     = intern(g,'Remap',[intern(g,'TexSample',[],{slot:'rough', uv:0})],{in:[0,1], out:[0.04,1]})
metal     = intern(g,'Slider',[],{value:0.0})
shade     = intern(g,'PBR',[albedoTex, rough, metal],{normals:'tangent'})

-- which variant do we need right now?
variantKey = hash(shade.id, entry:'frag', features: enabled, backend: adapter.info.backend,
                  precision: wantF16 ? 'f16' : 'f32',
                  pass: { color: ['bgra8unorm-srgb'], depth: 'depth24plus', blend:'none', samples: 4 })
if idb.has(variantKey): return idb.get(variantKey)          -- reuse GPUShaderModule + pipeline
wgsl = emit(shade)                                          -- per-node text cached by node.id
pipe = await device.createRenderPipelineAsync(compile(wgsl, features))
idb.put(variantKey, pipe.getBindGroupLayout?/module + layout)

-- cross-worker transfer of one material to a compile worker
postMessage({ defs: closure(g, shade.id) });   worker: g2 = new Graph; adopt(g2, defs)
applications.key_note: Note 5, the node id is not the cache key: the same `shade.id` yields a different binary under a different backend/adapter, precision, or render-pass state (formats, blend, depth, sample count), and reusing a pipeline compiled for the wrong state returns a wrong-looking material rather than an error. The variant key must therefore add all pipeline state and device identity, exactly as the originating project adds `scale | region | precision`.
applications.failure_or_adaptation: The pattern's unit of compilation does not match its unit of naming: WGSL compiles whole modules, so there is no per-node compiled artifact to cache. What pays off is (a) an interned whole-material id, because it makes 'is this material equal to the one in the asset?' a string compare instead of a structural diff, (b) per-node *emitted text* cached by node id, so editing one slider re-emits one node and re-links the module, and (c) hashing the final program to key the variant. Variant explosion from feature defines must be in the hash or two variants collide. The binary side of the cache is per-device and per-driver, so "same id" guarantees reuse only on the same adapter — the cache needs device partitioning and versioning of the compiler and of the WGSL emission code (an edited emission rule must change every key, or you return stale binaries). Hidden inputs are everywhere: `time`, viewport size, device pixel ratio, precision chosen by a quality setting, and the tangent-frame convention — all must be explicit arguments or uniforms. Finally the 52-bit number key is tempting in JS and dangerous here (a collision is a visibly wrong material); emit 64-char hex ids and keep the canonical bytes if you want collision detection.
